There are teachers, people who review school budgets, and people who study while working. Even when they face the same smartphone, they do not necessarily have the same concerns.

full_story_part2.text: In a classroom before class, I teach Japanese at a middle school and mark a text we want to discuss. If smartphones no longer distract us, could we focus more on the text? I do hope so. But what I want to protect, apart from test scores, is not just a quiet classroom. It is time to encounter, through words, a point of view different from my own. I look over the lesson plan on the teacher's desk. I don't want to cut the time we spend with the text by focusing only on checking whether phones are put away.

full_story_part3.text: As someone who reviews school budgets for a local government, I spread documents about device management and learning support across my desk and add sticky notes. Do I see this as money spent to reduce device use, or money spent to help students learn more? My hand stops as I write the review notes. I can't say one should take priority while that difference remains unclear. I'm afraid of cutting necessary support from a limited budget. I can't simply use findings from overseas as the answer for my own area. I have to explain what evidence I used to choose this allocation.

full_story_part3_c2.text: In an evening high school classroom after work, I take out my notebook and check whether there are any work messages on my phone. I want to avoid using it during class. Still, I can't say that I will stay away from messages no matter what happens. As an adult, I want to take responsibility for both my work and my studies. In the margin of my notebook, I write what I want to tell the school. Before it is decided that devices will be locked away, I want room to think about it too. I don't want to put in the bag my responsibility to manage how I use the device myself.

full_story_part3_c3.text: Everyone wants to value the time they spend learning. I think we agree on that. But when a decision is wrong, what people lose and how much they have to take on themselves are different. So we do not all have the same standard for saying it was a good choice. The power to decide where the money goes, the power to run a classroom, and the responsibility to manage one's own life are not the same thing. And even if you have little say in what is decided, the weight of the decision is not necessarily any lighter. Even if you have something deeply important to protect, that does not mean you will have a say in the decision. Whose understanding is still waiting to be put into words?
